To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neural mechanisms of speech understanding include the activation of left posterior inferior temporal lobe and left inferior frontal gyrus, and that these brain regions are activated by the semantic aspects of speech comprehension.
the semantic aspects of speech comprehension are subserved by a network of left and right fronto-temporal brain regions.
the semantic ambiguity of spoken words and sentences activates the left posterior inferior temporal lobe and the bilateral inferior frontal gyri.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional organization of the brain regions that are involved in spoken language processing.
the neural mechanisms of spoken language comprehension, and in particular with the role of the frontal and temporal lobes.
the functional neuroanatomy of language comprehension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the left posterior inferior temporal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus are involved in the resolution of semantic ambiguity in spoken language comprehension.
semantic ambiguity is a very powerful tool for the investigation of the neural basis of spoken language comprehension, and that this technique has provided us with a number of important insights.

the brain regions involved in semantic ambiguity are the same regions that have been identified in other semantic tasks, and that the neural mechanisms of speech processing and semantics are intimately linked.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

semantic ambiguity provides a useful tool for studying semantic processing, and that semantic ambiguity can be used to investigate the neural mechanisms of spoken language comprehension, and to test the functional role of specific brain regions in semantic processing.
the brain regions that subserve semantic comprehension are those that subserve semantic processing in general.

the neural mechanisms of speech perception and comprehension are more complex than previously thought, and that semantic ambiguity can be a useful tool in the functional neuroimaging investigation of these mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are regions of the brain that are involved in the computation of word meanings, and that these regions are activated even though the listener is unaware that the sentence is ambiguous.
the brain regions we have identified as playing a role in the semantic aspects comprehension are not only important for language, but are also involved in other aspects of cognition.

the semantic aspects of language comprehension are subserved by the fronto-temporo-parietal language network, and that these brain regions are involved not only in the processing of novel or unusual words, but in the processing of the most common words of the language.
